newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire reinforces on two fronts after rebel push.
newsitem.headline: Zaire reinforces on two fronts after rebel push.

text.p: Zaire's army was reinforcing on two fronts following a rebel push into its southern mineral-producing Shaba province, military officials and other sources said on Wednesday.
But its campaign to enlist 26,000 teenagers to help fight in the war in the east has begun slowly, with recruiting officers awaiting instructions on how to proceed.
"We are waiting for written instructions from the defence ministry before we begin the enrolement," a senior officer in the paramilitary gendarmerie told Reuters in Kinshasa.
He said that seven young hopefuls who had turned up at the national gendarmerie headquarters in the capital on Wednesday had been told to come back next week.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila told Reuters in Goma on Wednesday that veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko had until February 21 come start negotiations on handing over power or face a major rebel offensive.

Mobutu aides say he is on his way back to Zaire after further medical tests in Europe following prostate surgery there in August. He spent Tuesday and Wednesday in Morocco, which sent troops to help Mobutu crush Shaba revolts in the 1970s.
Zaire has repeatedly ruled out talks with the rebels, describing them as puppets of Rwanda and Uganda, two neighbours it accuses of invading its territory.

A military official, who asked not to be named, and sources within the region said that the army was reinforcing to push rebels out of the Shaba town of Kalemie on Lake Tanganyika and to defend Moba further south.
Transport sources said the railway was working to within about 50 km (30 miles) of Kalemie, which Zaire has acknowledged losing to the rebels on Monday.
Kalemie is a strategic commercial transit point with rail, air and lake connections to the entire region.
The military official said the army was also reinforcing at Lubutu on the road from Zaire's eastern border zone to Kisangani, headquarters for the counter-offensive the army launched on January 20.

The Tutsi-led rebels launched their revolt in October, accusing Zaire of denying them citizenship and seeking to return them to Rwanda, which their forebears left generations ago. The army counter-offensive has made little apparent headway.

The planned new recruits look unlikely to add an immediate boost. Some military sources say that with medical and aptitude tests and training, it could take several months to integrate them into the army.
The military official said mercenaries, many of them from former Yugoslavia, remained deployed much further north at the airport serving the rebel-held town of Watsa.
Estimates of the total size of the army and gendarmerie range from the official 100,000 soldiers to as low as 40,000.
Zaire's deputy foreign minister, Henri-Thomas Lokondo Yoka, on Tuesday ruled out talks despite the latest setbacks. "They may be winning battles but they have not won the war," he said.

In Europe, metal traders remained calm in the face of the escalation of hostilities into Shaba, saying the fighting was having no impact on production or exports from the main copper mining areas hundreds of km (miles) to the south.
